name: Dark Porcelain Green
lede: Dark Porcelain Green darkens [[porcelain-green]], named for the celadon glaze on East Asian porcelain, and in our archive it runs at over three times its normal rate in paintings from the 1900s.

sections.title: A darkened glaze green
sections.body:
The name pairs dark with [[porcelain-green]], which takes its own name from the grey-green celadon glazes fired onto East Asian porcelain [1]. Ridgway charted this darker tone in 1912 on plate XXXIII, hue 39′′, tone k, and the ISCC-NBS *Dictionary of Color Names* carried it forward in 1955 as block 163 [1].

Measured against our Color Graph, its nearest neighbor is [[japanese-blue]], 2.9 units away and a touch bluer; [[nickel-green]] is greener, and [[dark-russian-green]], a Japanese traditional color, is nearly the same, 3.3 units off [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A match for this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 193 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.8 per cent, as photographed [3]. Impressionist paintings carry it at 8.8 times the archive's overall rate, 10 of 140, and Jean-Jacques Henner's work at over 20 times, 3 of his 18 paintings [3]. The earliest dated match is Andrea di Bartolo's *Presentation of the Virgin in the Temple*, 1400, a floor on the color's age in painting rather than a claim of its first appearance [3]. As photographed: these are computed color matches on museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test [3].
